content.p: Renae Lawrence was the only woman among the nine Australians arrested in Bali in April 2005 over a plan to carry heroin out of Indonesia. She was caught at the airport with packages strapped to her body, admitted to an Indonesian court that she had carried the drugs, and was still sentenced to life in prison, a harsher term than the 20 years prosecutors had asked for. The sentence was later cut to 20 years, and with remissions she walked out of Bangli prison in November 2018 after about 13 years, the first of the nine to be freed. Back in Australia she faced a different reckoning: a stolen-car chase from the weeks before her arrest, which a Newcastle magistrate dealt with in February 2019.
content.h2: A life coming apart in Newcastle
content.p: Before Bali, Lawrence was a 27-year-old from the Newcastle suburb of Wallsend who had trained as a panel beater and later worked for a catering company. Friends told the Sydney Morning Herald that her decline began when a decade-long relationship with an older woman, Tracie Sansom, ended in October 2004. After the split she moved back in with her mother and stepfather. A foot injury needing workers' compensation had left her struggling, and a local football club reportedly told her she could not play until she paid her registration.

Money was tight. Her father, Robert, told reporters that her car had broken down and she was "desperate for money" to fix it; the Herald reported that the repair would cost at least $1,000, on top of car loan repayments and a growing credit card debt. He called her "gullible and naive" and said she was "probably 15" at heart. Psychologist Michael Carr-Gregg, quoted by the Herald, argued that young people from unsettled homes with little sense of belonging were exactly the kind of recruits a trafficker would choose.

The same coverage records an episode that came back to haunt her. At about 4.30 a.m. on 26 March 2005, police allege, Lawrence stole a car in Sydney and drove north with fellow Bali Nine member Matthew Norman, a catering colleague nine years younger. Police used road spikes to stop them on the Central Coast. The pair were due in Gosford court on car theft and traffic charges on the Tuesday after the Bali arrests became public.

Lawrence worked on catering shifts at the Sydney Cricket Ground alongside Andrew Chan, Matthew Norman and Martin Stephens, all four of whom were later arrested in Bali. A man who had worked with Chan told the Herald that Chan seemed to be drawing on his catering-company contacts to offer colleagues free trips to Bali. Lawrence's lawyer, Anggia Browne, said the couriers were to be paid between $10,000 and $15,000 for carrying heroin with a street value she put at $4 million.

Lawrence's own account, as she later told Indonesian police, put the first approach by Chan shortly before her 27th birthday in October 2004. The Age reported that, according to her police interviews, she made one earlier trip to Bali, had heroin strapped to her body for the flight back to Sydney and received thousands of dollars in cash. Prosecutor Putu Indriati asked her in January 2006 whether two earlier visits had also been smuggling runs. Lawrence denied it, though the court was told her passport showed her trips to Bali fell on the same dates as those of Chan and other members of the group. Her third trip, the one on which she was arrested, was paid for by Chan, she said.

On 17 April 2005, Indonesian police arrested Lawrence at Bali's airport. The Herald reported that she was taken with Stephens, Chan, Michael Czugaj and Scott Rush; police said heroin was strapped to the bodies of everyone except Chan, who was carrying none. Four others, Tan Duc Thanh Nguyen, Matthew Norman, Myuran Sukumaran and Si Yi Chen, were arrested the same night at a hotel in Kuta. Together the group was said to have been carrying 8.3 kilograms of heroin out of Indonesia. Reports put Lawrence's share at about 2.6 kilograms (Sydney Morning Herald and Canberra Times) or 2.7 kilograms (ABC and news.com.au).

Police video of her interrogation was broadcast in Australia within days. It showed the drugs being removed from her body and her telling other suspects she feared for her family if she named anyone. Her father said that after her arrest she phoned a step-brother, told him she had been pushed into the scheme, and that her family would have been harmed if she had refused.

In the Denpasar District Court the nine faced seven separate trials, each carrying a maximum penalty of death. Lawrence's case was heard in January 2006. "I'm guilty of carrying this stuff to Australia," she said, "but I'm not guilty of owning, selling or anything else because Andrew Chan owns it, not me." She told the judges that Chan had said only that he was having trouble "getting the stuff through the airport at Jakarta" and had asked her to delay her flight by a day. When the packages were strapped on, she guessed they held drugs: "Obviously, if they're having trouble getting something through an airport, it's illegal." But she said she did not know it was heroin, because "stuff could be anything."

She said she had been too frightened to pull out, because Chan had threatened to send her "to the farm". Testifying in December 2005 at the trial of Scott Rush, she said she was still afraid of Chan, who she said had boasted of having Australian police "on his payroll", and that she avoided him inside Kerobokan prison. Asked why she had not gone to police in Australia, she said she did not trust them. She also alleged that a woman called Grace, Chan's girlfriend, had packed the strapping materials. The court heard that all four couriers made similar claims of threats from Chan and Sukumaran.

Lawrence cooperated from the start on her lawyers' advice. Prosecutors asked for 20 years, the lowest term sought for any of the nine, and she had come to court believing she could receive as little as 15. In February 2006 the judges instead gave her life. The Age wrote that a stunned Lawrence asked her lawyer: "Can they do that?"

The next day, Chan and Sukumaran were sentenced to death by firing squad (Sukumaran in a later hearing), and Stephens and Czugaj received life terms. Judge Arief Supratman, the Herald reported, dismissed the claims that four defendants had been forced to carry drugs by threats against their families. Prime Minister John Howard said it was beyond him how anyone could be "so stupid", and Foreign Minister Alexander Downer disclosed that ministers had privately pleaded with Indonesia against the death penalty. Australian Federal Police commissioner Mick Keelty defended his agency's decision to tip off Indonesian police: "We'd do the same thing again."

The BBC reported that Bali's high court later cut the terms of several of the couriers, including Lawrence, then 28, and Czugaj, 20, whom the deputy chief judge, Hyster Arsan Pardede, called "only couriers". The death sentences on Chan and Sukumaran were upheld. The court spokesman said the purpose of the punishments was "not to seek revenge but to give defendants chances to fix their lives." Lawrence's life term became 20 years.

She spent her years first in Kerobokan prison, then in Negara, and finally in Bangli. The Canberra Times reported that Indonesia hands out sentence reductions twice a year, on religious holidays and on Independence Day, and that Lawrence received a series of them. In 2015 she told Fairfax Media that she had been deeply affected by the executions of Chan and Sukumaran on 29 April of that year, and that she hoped to be released one day. To cope with the isolation she took up gardening as a form of therapy.

By late 2018 she stood apart from the rest of the group. Si Yi Chen, Michael Czugaj, Matthew Norman, Scott Rush and Martin Stephens were still serving life sentences. Four of them had applied every year since 2012 to have life converted to a fixed term, a change needing President Joko Widodo's personal approval, and none had been granted. The ninth, Tan Duc Thanh Nguyen, had died of cancer in 2018; the Canberra Times gave June and the Herald gave May.

The head of Bali's provincial corrections division, Slamet Prihantoro, announced in mid-November 2018 that Lawrence would be released on 21 November and handed to immigration for deportation. Then 41, she was freed after more than 12 years behind bars. Days before she landed, the Herald reported that she faced arrest over warrants from Gosford Local Court for the March 2005 incident, which had remained outstanding. She was photographed arriving at Brisbane airport in November 2018 and, according to news.com.au, soon handed herself in to police over the charges.

In January 2019 her lawyer, Drew Hamilton, entered guilty pleas at Newcastle Local Court to car theft, driving without a licence, speeding and failing to stop for police. The court was told she had stolen a white Ford Laser in Enfield and reached 130 km/h in a 90 km/h zone before being stopped at Mooney Mooney. Court documents said she had suffered anxiety and depression since her return.

On 5 February 2019 Magistrate Sharon Crews fined her $1,000 and placed her on a 12-month Community Corrections Order. Hamilton said she had undergone significant rehabilitation in Indonesia and struggled with drug abuse when she committed the offences but was not otherwise known to police. He said she was "a different person" from the one who should have appeared in 2005. The police prosecutor said that had the matter been dealt with in 2005 police would have sought "a significant penalty", but accepted that 13 years had passed. The magistrate said she hoped Lawrence would approach life with "promise and hope".
